messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 64
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Warehouse Worker
  trauma_type: Captivity
  pcl5: 60

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Time of Day: The same time of day the event occurred, Animal Phobia: Talks or photos about snakes, Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Sleep: Going to sleep or lying in the dark, Reassurance Seeking: I keep asking others to reassure me that I am okay, Body Monitoring: constantly check body for signs of danger or injury
  Threat: Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Negative Appraisals: Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it

Vignette:
Mr. Rajan, a 64-year-old South Asian man married for over forty years, has been struggling with the aftermath of his captivity experience for several months now. The trauma he endured was deeply rooted in a situation where he was held against his will by individuals who had taken control of the warehouse where he worked. This event occurred at around midnight, leaving him particularly vulnerable and helpless. The memory of that night is still vivid; Mr. Rajan had been working late to complete an urgent shipment when several masked men entered the warehouse. They bound him and kept him confined for hours, making threats and demands that left him feeling completely powerless. The same time of day now triggers intense anxiety, a reminder of the fear he experienced during those dark hours. Since then, Mr. Rajan has found it increasingly difficult to sleep at night. Lying in the darkness evokes a sense of dread, and he often wakes up drenched in sweat, his heart racing as if reliving that moment. He avoids going to bed or lying down in the dark, preferring instead to stay awake through the night. This avoidance has led to significant disruptions in his sleep patterns, leaving him exhausted during the day and unable to concentrate on his work. Mr. Rajan’s marriage has also been affected by these changes. His wife, worried about his constant state of alertness and reluctance to rest at night, often tries to reassure him that he is safe now. He frequently seeks her comfort, asking if she thinks he will be okay or if the nightmares will ever stop. This reliance on reassurance has strained their relationship; Mr. Rajan feels guilty for burdening his wife with his fears but cannot seem to find solace without her constant affirmation. The fear of snakes—a symbol that emerged during his captivity—also haunts him. One day, while watching a television show about wildlife, he encountered an image of a snake and was immediately transported back to the warehouse, feeling trapped and helpless again. This has led Mr. Rajan to avoid any media or conversations related to reptiles. Mr. Rajan’s hypervigilance is another aspect that affects his daily life. He remains on high alert at all times, constantly scanning his surroundings for signs of danger. His nights are the most difficult; he struggles to feel safe and frequently checks behind him, convinced that someone might be following him or watching him from the shadows. His negative appraisals contribute significantly to his distress. Mr. Rajan believes that he cannot prevent bad things from happening to him again and sometimes questions whether his life is worth living anymore. The thought of re-experiencing that level of fear and helplessness is too much for him to bear, leading him to actively avoid thinking about the event altogether. What frightens Mr. Rajan most is the constant sense of threat and danger that pervades every aspect of his life now. He has come to believe that he will never be truly safe again, a notion reinforced by the recurrence of nightmares and intrusive thoughts at specific times of day. Despite these challenges, Mr. Rajan feels an urgent need for help. His wife encouraged him to seek professional support after noticing the severe toll this trauma has taken on his physical and emotional well-being. He is hopeful that with the right guidance, he can regain some sense of control over his life and feel safe again. His primary goal is to learn how to manage his fears without constantly feeling like a prisoner in his own mind.
